suggestions.rationale: Depression is a common psychiatric comorbidity in multiple sclerosis, but prevalence evidence does not establish that MS caused an individual's depressive disorder. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 58 articles including 87,756 patients with MS estimated pooled depression prevalence at 30.5%, while a later meta-analysis reported 27.01% across MS populations and substantial variation by clinical subgroup and measurement method. This mapping therefore supports association/comorbidity research only; individual chronology, disability burden, fatigue, pain, sleep, cognition, medication exposure, psychosocial factors, and other psychiatric causes require case-specific review.
evidenceGaps: Neurology documentation confirming multiple sclerosis phenotype, course, and disability context
Depressive-disorder diagnosis, severity, and chronology relative to MS symptoms and diagnosis
Fatigue, pain, sleep, cognitive, functional, medication, and psychosocial contributors
History of depressive symptoms predating MS or another independent psychiatric disorder
Qualified clinician assessment distinguishing common MS/depression comorbidity from individual causation or aggravation

sourceReferences.citation: Boeschoten RE, Braamse AMJ, Beekman ATF, et al. Prevalence of depression and anxiety in Multiple Sclerosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Neurol Sci. 2017;372:331-341. PMID 28017241
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review/meta-analysis of 58 articles and 87,756 patients with MS estimated pooled depression prevalence at 30.5% and emphasized heterogeneity across methods and populations. Supports association/comorbidity research, not individual causal attribution.
